items.title: fix: make main authoritative for HyperMeow
items.body:
## Summary

- add a public changelog and evidence-linked README comparison with upstream WhatsMeow
- remove the long module/package and duplicate-descriptor explanation from the README
- retract accidental `v0.1.0` and the required `v0.1.1` retraction carrier
- use `@main` for the newest reviewed pseudo-version; `v0.0.0` remains the only selectable tag
- keep `dev` as an integration branch that never publishes or indexes versions
- consolidate all handwritten business-app features into `business.go`
- move retained benchmark evidence into `benchmark/barback/testdata/results`
- consolidate 30 root white-box test files into five themed files, retaining the external suite
- preserve MPL-2.0 for upstream-derived content and license Polymorfa-authored files under Rajeh Taher MIT

## Licensing boundary

- files and source content inherited from `tulir/whatsmeow` history retain MPL-2.0
- Polymorfa modifications inside inherited files remain MPL-2.0
- all 43 Go files authored by Polymorfa carry the Rajeh Taher MIT header
- every other commentable Polymorfa-authored file carries the same MIT notice
- Docker syntax directives remain first, followed immediately by the MIT notice
- generated, benchmark-data, and other non-commentable Polymorfa artifacts are covered by `LICENSE-MIT` and `LICENSING.md`
- consolidated upstream-derived `business.go` retains Tulir Asokan copyright and MPL-2.0

## Version correction

Go proxies cannot discover an untagged pseudo-version through `@latest` when every tagged version is retracted. After this PR is approved and merge-committed to `main`, create `v0.1.1` on this exact reviewed PR head as the self-retracted correction carrier and create `v0.0.0` on the reviewed `main` merge commit as the only selectable tag. Do not create a GitHub Release. `@latest` then resolves `v0.0.0`; `@main` resolves the newest reviewed main commit to its pseudo-version.

## Preservation proofs

- repository-wide Test/Benchmark/Fuzz/Example declaration inventory hash matches `main`
- covered statements and total statements exactly match `main` (2,288 / 40,324)
- exported Go documentation hash is unchanged by the business source consolidation
- root test-file count is reduced from 31 to 6 without removing test behavior

## Verification

- `pre-commit run --all-files`
- generated MEX check
- `go build ./...`
- `go test ./...`
- `go test -race ./...`

items.title: fix(bench): gate #82 on the median ratio with a per-size floor
items.body:
Resolves #327.

## Summary

`run_gate` failed if **any** single size fell below the threshold — it gated on the minimum, the noisiest statistic available. Two runs of the identical protocol, same binaries and pinning, on the same idle machine, failed at **disjoint sets of sizes**, so the verdict was decided by noise rather than by the kernel.

| statistic | run A | run B | swing |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| **median of ratios** | 82.3% | 82.5% | **0.2 pt** |
| mean | 82.1% | 82.2% | 0.1 pt |
| min (the old rule) | 76.3% | 78.7% | 2.4 pt |
| worst single size | — | — | **6.2 pt** |

The gate now asserts the **median** ≥ `--threshold` (0.80), with a new `--floor` (0.70) that no individual size may drop below. The median is ~30× more stable and matches what the epic actually claims — "within 10–20% of OpenBLAS" is an aggregate statement, not a per-size one. The floor keeps the rule honest: a genuine cliff still fails, while ±6-point noise does not.

## Changes

- `benchmarks/analyze_gate.py` — median-based gate, `--floor`, summary line (median/mean/min/max), per-size marks demoted to `ok`/`low`/`FLOOR` where only `FLOOR` is fatal. Validation rejects `--floor > --threshold`. The rationale and the numbers above are recorded in the docstring so the choice is not re-litigated from scratch.
- `benchmarks/README.md` — new "What the gate asserts, and why" section with the stability table.
- `benchmarks/data/README.md` — reproduction command updated.
- `docs/benchmarks/i7-12700k.md` — reported the gate as **FAILING**; now reports PASS at 82.3% with the aggregation rationale.

## Verification

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Run A (committed CSVs) | **PASS** — median 82.3%, exit 0 |
| Run B (independent re-run) | **PASS** — median 82.5%, exit 0 |
| Synthetic 50% cliff at N=705 | **FAIL** on floor, exit 1 |
| `--threshold 0.90` | **FAIL** on median |
| `--floor 0.9 --threshold 0.8` | rejected by argparse |
| `--reference blis` | PASS, median 84.1% |
| Table mode (non-gate path) | unchanged |
| `python3 -m py_compile` | clean |

The cliff case is the one that justifies the floor: the median stayed at 81.4% and would have passed on its own, but the floor caught it.

No gcc/clang build in the test matrix because **no C++ changed** — this PR touches one Python script and three Markdown files. `npm run build` for the docs site still produces 43 pages.

## One correction to the issue

#327 proposed "more iterations" as a variance fix. The data says otherwise: within-run stddev is already only **0.3–2.2%** of the median at 10 iterations. The variance is *between* runs (turbo/thermal state, allocation, page layout), not within them, so more iterations would cost time and change nothing. Recorded in the docstring and the README so it isn't retried. The remaining real lever is the `powersave` governor.

## Test plan

- [ ] CI passes
- [ ] Promote to ready when satisfied: `gh pr ready <N>`

items.title: bench: track benchmark results over time (long-term trend store) (closes #51)
items.body:
Closes #51. Builds on #50's generator to retain benchmark results **over time**, so drift across many `main` commits is visible — not just the current snapshot or a single PR's base↔head delta.

## Shaping decision

**Option 2 — committed CSV/raw results + benchstat** (over github-action-benchmark). A git-native, zero-dependency store that reuses the existing `benchreport` generator and benchstat, matching the repo's self-contained ethos: no `gh-pages` branch, no JS action dependency. Rationale recorded in `docs/bench/history/README.md` and the CI/Makefile comments.

**Retention:** hard cap of 100 snapshots; the oldest are pruned on each push to bound repo growth.

## How it works

The store is one snapshot per push to `main`: `docs/bench/history/<timestamp>_<sha>.txt`, holding the **raw, multi-sample** `go test -bench` output. That format is deliberate:

- **Significance is recoverable** — keeping every sample (not just benchstat's median) lets the regression check run a real statistical test between commits, rather than comparing untrustworthy single deltas.
- **benchstat reads them directly** — the documented manual recipe (`benchstat <old>.txt <new>.txt`) works with no preprocessing (verified locally).

New code in the `tools/benchreport` module (its own dependency-free module, outside the root 100% coverage gate):

- **`stats.go`** — standard-library Mann–Whitney U test (normal approximation, tie + continuity correction), so significance needs no benchstat shell-out.
- **`history.go`** — raw-bench parser → per-cell ns/op sample sets; sortable snapshot names; `AddHistoryEntry` with hard-cap pruning; `LoadHistory`.
- **`trend.go`** — the `## Trend` section (median ns/op per headline across recent commits, newest-first), a **report-only regression check** requiring a **significant (p<0.05), >10%, two-consecutive-comparison** slowdown before flagging, plus the manual benchstat recipe.
- **`main.go` / `render.go`** — new `history` subcommand; `render` gains `-history`/`-alert`; README deep-links the trend section once history exists.

**Wiring:**
- **Makefile** — opt-in `BENCH_HISTORY=1` archive step (only the consistent CI environment feeds the store; a maintainer's local reference run doesn't pollute it); `bench-render` always reads the store.
- **CI** — the main-only `bench-report` job archives each commit, appends the regression verdict to the run summary, and commits `docs/bench/history/`.

Report-only throughout — a regression *gate* stays out of scope until a low-noise runner exists (consistent with #50's documented path).

## Verification

- New logic well-covered by `stats_test.go` / `history_test.go` / `trend_test.go`; module `gofmt`/`vet`/tests pass; root module build/vet/tests unaffected.
- End-to-end render against a simulated 3-commit store produced the trend table, legend, regression verdict, recipe, and README link.
- Confirmed benchstat parses the snapshot files natively.

Feature is wired but **dormant until the first `main` push** populates the store — no synthetic data committed, so `BENCHMARKS.md`/`README.md` are untouched until CI re-renders with real history.

items.title: Solver diagnostics: turn-landmark archetype, transposition table, repair-search stagnation + corpus-2 refresh correction
items.body:
## Summary

Continued diagnostic work on the `dfs-plain`/turn-landmark archetype solver gap, plus a critical correction to a false claim from earlier today's corpus-2 refresh. No solver source code is shipped by this PR — every speculative code change was implemented, tested, measured, and reverted (see each commit/report for the full cycle).

**Diagnostic findings (all with real, measured evidence, most negative results):**
- `adjTurnDeadlocked` — generalized `mustTurn`'s deadlock-feasibility check to `adjacentTurn` landmarks. Sound, unit-tested, `solver:bench --check` clean — but measured at **zero fires across ~88.7M evaluations** on 6 diverse levels. Reverted.
- Closed the "real attempt-policy profile" witness-divergence gap flagged by earlier reports: using each level's actual selected profile instead of a generic baseline changes nothing (18/18 levels) — but `maxStepRank` ≤3 everywhere confirms per-step move quality isn't the bottleneck for `dfs-plain`/`repair-close`.
- Investigated a transposition-table premise: a crude state signature showed 92-99% "duplicate" node visits (looked like the biggest lever of the campaign). Following up with the *actually-sound* signature (full visited-cell identity + edge history) found the real rate is only 0.5-16% — corrected the same day before the inflated number could mislead anyone.
- First diagnosis of `repair-search.ts`'s own mechanism (everything prior examined DFS/beam): found a severe stagnation plateau (85-99% of budget wasted after an early quick improvement). Tested the obvious fix (longer stagnation burst) directly — net-negative (18/40 levels regressed vs. 4 improved, avg badness +16%), reverted.

**Critical correction — the 286/1700 corpus-2 refresh from earlier today never actually ran the repair-probe fixes.** The 20 `stress-corpus2-batch-NN` branches from the *prior* refresh still existed (branch deletion isn't available in this session), so the batch workflow's checkout logic continued from each branch's own stale pre-fix history instead of forking fresh from `main` — meaning the "fresh" run silently executed 2026-07-16 solver code the entire time, missing both repair-probe budget fix commits. Confirmed directly (`git merge-base --is-ancestor` against every sampled batch branch, byte-identical stale-vs-"fresh" checkpoint comparison, live reproduction via both a standalone script and the real `portfolio-solve-sweep.mjs` tool). Fixed by force-resetting all 20 batch branches to `main`'s tip (bringing in the real fixes) with a fresh checkpoint-archive commit on each, then re-triggering all 20 workflows — currently in progress. Corrected every doc/report that cited the false "286/1700, post repair-probe fixes" claim (`CLAUDE.md`, the roadmap, `data/stress/README.md`, the corpus2-batch README) to flag it as invalid pending the genuine re-run.

## Test plan

- [x] `tsc --noEmit` clean
- [x] `npx vitest run modules/solver` — 196/196 (net zero solver-source changes; every experimental change was reverted before commit)
- [x] `npm run solver:bench -- --check` — 160/160, no regressions (checked at multiple points, including with each experimental change temporarily in place)
- [x] `npm run check:no-solver-level-numbers` — passes
- [x] `git diff`/`git status` confirmed clean against every touched solver source file after each revert
- [ ] Genuine corpus-2 refresh (20 batches, currently running against the now-fixed branches) — not yet complete; will be combined and the docs updated with real numbers in a follow-up

items.title: docs: reconcile the README Vite and Nuxt benchmark rows with the snapshot
items.body: ## The defect The README table and the generated Blacksmith snapshot published **different numbers for the same two surfaces**, both presented as current: | Surface | `README.md` | `bench/results/tool-benchmark-latest.json` / `performance-blacksmith.md` | | --- | --- | --- | | Vite build | `1.70s` / `1.52s` / **1.1×** | `1.66s` / `732.5ms` / **2.3×** (1,000 files) | | Nuxt build | `6.68s` / `7.35s` / **0.9×** | `6.79s` / `6.42s` / **1.1×** (500 files) | That is not rounding — they are different runs. A reader got a different answer depending on which page they opened, and the README's version was the pessimistic one on both rows. Second, separate problem: the README header asserted > Measured on Blacksmith `blacksmith-32vcpu-ubuntu-2404`, **15,000 generated Vue SFCs**, median of 5 runs as a blanket claim, but only SFC compile, Lint, and Format run at 15,000. From the snapshot's own `surfaces[].files`: Type check **500**, Vite build **1,000**, Nuxt build **500**. The overstatement applied to exactly the three rows that look weakest. ## The change - The **Vite build** and **Nuxt build** rows now come from `bench/results/tool-benchmark-latest.json` — the artifact `docs/content/architecture/performance-blacksmith.md` is rendered from — and the table names that run ([29010164013](https://github.com/ubugeeei-prod/vize/actions/runs/29010164013)) rather than leaving one global link that does not apply to them. - A per-row **Files** column, populated from each surface's own `files` value. - The Nuxt row carries a **pending regeneration** marker. **No number in this PR is invented.** Every cell comes from the committed artifact. Where a fresh measurement is needed, the cell is marked rather than estimated. ## The Nuxt row is marked, not replaced #3409 shows the Nuxt benchmark let `@vizejs/nuxt` inherit a warm persistent pre-compile cache through a `node_modules` symlink shared by every run and both variants — a cache the Nuxt default compiler has no counterpart for. The `1.1×` in the artifact was measured under that harness. **The correction runs against Vize**: the honest cold-vs-cold figure is *worse* than `1.1×`, not better. The row is therefore footnoted as pending a fresh Blacksmith run once #3409 is on `main`. I have not substituted a local estimate, and the local runs I do have are not comparable — my machine was under heavy competing load throughout. ## Scope The **type-check row is deliberately untouched** — it is being retracted separately as an invalid cross-engine ratio (`vue-tsc` is the JavaScript TypeScript compiler, `vize check` is native tsgo). The compile/lint/format rows are from run 29004198781 and are not reconciled here; the table now says so instead of implying one provenance for everything. ## Test `tests/tooling/readme-benchmark-rows.test.ts` — two cases, both `assert.deepEqual` over whole rows so a failure shows the entire expected row: 1. the README's Vite and Nuxt rows equal the rows derived from `bench/results/tool-benchmark-latest.json`, formatted with the same `formatMs` rule the snapshot uses; 2. the header does not assert one corpus size, and every row's Files cell equals that surface's `files` in the artifact. Both **fail on the pre-fix README**, verified by stashing only `README.md`: ``` ✖ the README Vite and Nuxt rows match the committed benchmark snapshot actual: [ undefined, undefined ] expected: [ [ 'Vite build', '1,000', '@vitejs/plugin-vue', '1.66s', '732.5ms', '**2.3×**' ], [ 'Nuxt build', '500', 'Nuxt compiler', '6.79s', '6.42s', '**1.1×**†' ] ] ✖ the README states a per-row corpus size instead of one blanket figure actual: true expected: false ℹ pass 0 ℹ fail 2 ``` and pass after: ``` ✔ the README Vite and Nuxt rows match the committed benchmark snapshot ✔ the README states a per-row corpus size instead of one blanket figure ℹ pass 2 ℹ fail 0 ``` The existing `tests/tooling/readme-boundary.test.ts` still passes (2/2), so the README stays within its size and funnel constraints. ## Gates ``` $ nix develop -c vp run fmt:check # exit 0 $ nix develop -c vp run source:lengths # exit 0 ``` No Rust changed. Should land after #3409. Refs #3363 --- Need help on this PR? Tag @codesmith-bot with what you need. Autofix is enabled.

items.title: Update benchmark results after fixing top_k/remove_seen in recommend_k_* helpers
items.body:
## Summary

Follow-up to #2322, which fixed `top_k` and `remove_seen` being ignored in several `recommend_k_*` helpers in `examples/06_benchmarks/benchmark_utils.py`.

This PR reruns `movielens.ipynb` with the corrected code and updates the Algorithm Comparison table in `README.md` accordingly. It also cleans up several issues found during the rerun:

- Remove TensorFlow import block — none of the active algorithms (ALS, SAR, NCF, embdotbias, BPR, BiVAE, LightGCN) depend on TF.
- Remove all surprise/SVD dead code from `benchmark_utils.py` (import + 4 functions) and `movielens.ipynb` (commented-out blocks in 7 cells), since SVD is not in core dependencies.
- Split the single GPU `try/except` import block in `benchmark_utils.py` into three independent blocks (LightGCN, NCF, embdotbias) so a failure in one model's imports does not silently prevent the others from loading — this was the root cause of a `NameError: name 'RecoDataLoader' is not defined` during the rerun.
- Update the machine description (24 CPUs, GeForce RTX 5090 Laptop GPU with 24Gb).
- Minor notebook cleanup: add colons to markdown section headers, remove orphaned commented-out stubs.
- **Add `RATING_THRESHOLD = 3.5` for BPR**: BPR is an implicit feedback model and should not treat all ratings equally. Ratings >= 4 are binarized to 1 (positive) and ratings <= 3 are excluded. This threshold is applied consistently to both training data (via `prepare_training_bpr`) and test data (via `prepare_metrics_bpr`). The `remove_seen` masking still uses the full unfiltered training set so that all previously seen items are suppressed from recommendations.
- **Fix `BPR.recommend_k_items`**: seen-item masking (via `-inf`) is now applied to the score matrix *before* `argpartition`, guaranteeing exactly `top_k` valid recommendations per user. The old implementation filtered after selection, which could return fewer than `top_k` results when seen items appeared in the top-k window.
- Move `RATING_THRESHOLD` constant to module level (top of `benchmark_utils.py`) alongside other module constants.

## Metric changes

| Algo | Old MAP | New MAP | Old nDCG | New nDCG | Change |
|------|---------|---------|----------|----------|--------|
| ALS | 0.0047 | 0.0104 | 0.0442 | 0.0328 | within noise |
| BiVAE | 0.1461 | 0.3300 | 0.4751 | 0.4717 | large MAP increase — old run used different params |
| **BPR** | 0.1325 | **0.2292** | 0.4420 | **0.3623** | see note below |
| embdotbias | 0.0190 | 0.0549 | 0.1178 | 0.1190 | within noise |
| LightGCN | 0.0885 | 0.2772 | 0.4198 | 0.4191 | within noise |
| NCF | 0.1077 | 0.2603 | 0.3961 | 0.3931 | within noise |
| SAR | 0.1106 | 0.2585 | 0.3825 | 0.3938 | within noise |
| SVD | removed | — | removed | — | dropped with surprise |

**BPR note:** Two independent corrections affect the BPR result:

1. The old nDCG of 0.44 was artificially inflated because `recommend_k_items` was called without `top_k`, so the evaluator received a differently-ordered full candidate set rather than a top-10 list. Fixing this alone brought nDCG to ~0.197.
2. Applying `RATING_THRESHOLD = 3.5` (ratings >= 4 as positive) is methodologically correct for BPR, which is an implicit feedback model — treating low ratings as positive inflates metrics because BPR ignores rating magnitude entirely. With the threshold, nDCG rises to **0.3623** because the model now trains on a cleaner positive signal and is evaluated against the same filtered ground truth.

SAR rating metrics (RMSE/MAE/R²) are now shown as N/A — SAR does not produce rating predictions and never should have had those columns populated.

## Test plan

- `python -m py_compile examples/06_benchmarks/benchmark_utils.py`
- Full rerun of `examples/06_benchmarks/movielens.ipynb` on Movielens 100k — output committed.

FYI @he-yufeng

items.title: Audit the docs against recent PRs, and give each claim one owner
items.body:
# Audit the docs against recent PRs, and give each claim one owner

## Type of Change
- [ ] New feature
- [ ] Bug fix
- [x] Documentation update
- [ ] Refactoring
- [ ] Security patch
- [ ] Test coverage

## Description

Implements **PR 17 -- Docs & repo hygiene** from #54 ("Audit AGENTS.md against recent PRs; prune stale benchmark results").

Two distinct problems turned up, and the second was the larger one.

**Recent PRs left assertions behind that are now false.** The one that matters most is in `AGENTS.md`: it lists the genre skills that must run the citation gate, and it names four of the five. `deep-research` has been missing from that sentence since it was added, so the repository's own statement of its hard invariant reads as exempting a skill from it. Everything else -- `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, `DIAGRAMS.md`, `WRITING-STANDARDS.md` -- says five.

**One fact was being described by five documents, and main had just made it worse.** 24f4007 added an artifact-by-artifact reproducibility contract to `ARCHITECTURE.md`, explicitly "replacing four documents that each described one corner of it" -- but it added the canonical section without removing the four. So there were five, and the older ones disagree with the new measurement. `PERFORMANCE.md` still asserted *"repeating a run at the same worker count reproduces exactly"*, which 24f4007's own `repro_check.py` run falsifies (5 of 572 same-configuration comparisons differ in bytes, 2 in passage text). `PDF-PARSER.md` still carried the retracted "6 of 501 files, under 0.06%" figure and said retrieval was the only thing affected -- which understates the finding, since what actually changes is sometimes the quoted span itself.

That is the shape of most of this PR: not rewriting, but deciding which document owns a claim and pointing the others at it.

**On pruning benchmark results:** I did not delete any. `bench/results/` is 532 KB total and every directory is still cited by a dated section of `RESULTS.md`; deleting the raw data would break the evidence chain the directory exists to maintain, and `PARALLELISM-PLAN.md` makes "six intermediate conclusions were wrong" the explicit point of keeping them. The real staleness was that a reader had to reach a retraction *mid-document* to learn a number was withdrawn. `RESULTS.md` now opens with a table marking each section current, partly superseded, or superseded. Happy to actually delete data if you'd rather -- say the word.

## What changed, from the user's point of view

**Corrections**
- `AGENTS.md` names all five genre skills as bound by the citation gate, and all three review aids (`citation_provenance` was missing).
- `AGENTS.md` no longer claims a JDK is available and needed -- GROBID, the only thing that wanted one, was removed 2026-08-01.
- `AGENTS.md` no longer contradicts `CLI.md` on `--target host|docker`, which is informational only.
- `PERFORMANCE.md`'s reproducibility claim is corrected and the retracted figures are marked as retracted rather than removed, since they were quoted elsewhere.

**One owner per claim**
- `ARCHITECTURE.md`'s contract (added by 24f4007) is now the single statement of what is reproducible. `DESIGN.md`, `PARALLELISM.md`, `PDF-PARSER.md` and `PERFORMANCE.md` point at it.
- `PERFORMANCE.md` owns the reference-machine specifications it is the only consumer of; `README.md` links to them.

**`DESIGN.md` redraft**
- Cut "Design pattern review" -- six named patterns containing no decision, whose one concrete part (a module responsibility list) duplicates `DEVELOPER.md`'s more current one.
- Moved the five "Design improvement recommendations" to #54, where four are already sequenced PRs (6, 7, 9, 16). Posting them as an issue comment rather than deleting -- see below.
- Added a scope statement, a table of contents, and a title that describes the file.

**`README.md` hardware requirements**
- Trimmed to sizing. The two install traps (a CPU-only host pulling several GB of unused CUDA packages; a GPU host where `torch.cuda.is_available()` is `False`) moved to a new `PERFORMANCE.md` section -- they are install failure modes, not requirements.
- Scale is kept explicitly: 501 PDFs / 13,400 pages parses in ~4 minutes on the multi-GPU machine against 1h 56m serially, and tens of minutes on ordinary hardware.

**`DEVELOPER.md`**
- Benchmark headline refreshed (it still led with the superseded 2.46x) and the 2026-08-07 passage-reproducibility finding added.
- Repo layout tree corrected: it opened `README.md   you are here` *inside `DEVELOPER.md`*, and omitted `bench/repro_check.py`, `LADDERS.md`, `WRITING-STANDARDS.md` and `NAME.md`.

**New in `AGENTS.md`: "Conventions a new stage has to follow"** -- three rules that existed only in commit messages: per-document progress reporting from anything holding the write lock (#50, #58), classifying a failure by an exception mark rather than by matching its message (#55), and treating a partial parse as a failure.

## Test plan

- [x] Full suite with coverage: **1025 passed, 2 skipped, 100% line and branch** (`.venv-full/bin/python -m pytest --cov=src --cov=scripts --cov-report=term-missing`).
- [x] `poetry check` -- All set!
- [x] End-to-end smoke test: `scripts/release.py` builds `chitragupta-3.3.4.zip`, and the archive still ships all 14 `docs/*.md` while excluding `AGENTS.md`, `DEVELOPER.md`, `tests/` and `bench/` -- which is exactly the claim `README.md` makes about it, so this verifies the change and the documentation together.
- [x] Link/anchor check across all 31 markdown files: every internal link and every `#anchor` resolves. This caught one real break (`PDF-PARSER.md` pointed at the `PERFORMANCE.md` section this PR renames) which is fixed here.

**Unrelated pre-existing issue found while running the suite, not fixed here:** `tests/test_config.py::TestModuleReloadWithEnvOverrides::test_parser_ocr_defaults_off` asserts `PARSER_OCR is False` but reloads the real `src.config`, so it reads the host's `config.toml` rather than the tracked default. It passes against `config.toml.example` and fails on any host that sets `ocr = true`. Worth a `monkeypatch` of `CONFIG_PATH`; happy to open a separate issue.

Docs-only, so **PATCH** -> 3.3.4.

Closes the PR 17 item of #54.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

## Update: rebased onto #61, plus two documents brought in from outside the repo

**Rebased onto `c3f3558` (#61, merged).** Only `pyproject.toml` conflicted; resolved to **3.4.1**. Two follow-ups that #61 made necessary:

- `DEVELOPER.md`'s "unbuilt features" listed scheduling, log files and cron's environment as missing. 3.4.0 shipped all three (and #61 went beyond PR 11's scope into PR 12's cron/systemd docs). Only bib-file freshness is genuinely open now — and it isn't a coding task, so it's stated as such.
- `AGENTS.md`'s new progress-reporting convention needed to record *where* output goes, since #61 split it: `sync`'s stdout is a pinned contract, so its progress and warnings now go through `logging` to `logs/sync.log`, while the enrichment stages still `print`. `logs/` added to the repo layout.

### New: `docs/GROBID-CITATION-GRAPH.md`

The proposal attached to #22, updated from the pre-3.0.0 layout it was written against (`src/heavy/` → `src/enrich/`, `scripts/full_pipeline.py` → `scripts/enrich.py`, "job 1"/"job 2" → the layer names, `[heavy]` → `[enrich]`), with both ASCII box charts replaced by mermaid — **rendered with mermaid-cli to confirm they parse**, not just written and hoped for.

Two substantive corrections, not just renames:

- **It reversed a decision without mentioning it.** GROBID was removed on 2026-08-01, and `PDF-PARSER.md` named the *one* case worth revisiting: `/api/processFulltextDocument` for reference lists, as opposed to the header endpoint that was actually wired up. The proposal is exactly that case — so it now opens by quoting the removal and showing it qualifies, and keeps the operational objection (pinned JDK 21, Gradle build, service on 8070) rather than dropping it. It is also marked clearly as **a proposal, not a plan**; `[grobid]` is not a setting that exists.
- **Its citekey-invariant argument had inverted.** It justified external citation-graph nodes by analogy with `papers/pdfs/` — a second, uncitable namespace that was *deleted* in 3.3.0 because every downstream stage paid for it. The analogy now argues the opposite: don't reintroduce one. Added the citekey-as-filename rule from 3.3.1, which anything writing `content/grobid/<citekey>.tei.xml` inherits.

I also added "What it would cost" and "Open questions", including the one that seems decisive: `content/topics.json` is already an artifact nothing reads. A second unread artifact, bought with a JDK and a long-running service, would be a worse version of the same mistake — so a named consumer should exist before this is built.

While in that file I also found **two more instances of the "tokenises on whitespace" error** Copilot caught, and a 4.19%/4.17% disagreement within the same document.

items.title: docs(bench): report ingest, train, total
items.body:
## Summary

Presentation half of #301: perf tables report `ingest_s` and `train_s` beside `fit_s` wherever the underlying committed rows carry them, not just the total. This is renderer-only; the runner change that will populate bonsai's split (`Dataset(..., device=...)` binning on the device before `train(pairs, ds)`) is separate work, tracked by #301 itself and owned by another agent right now.

## Where the split landed

Four standings axes carry `ingest_s`/`train_s` today: rows (`rebaseline-2026-08.jsonl`), width (`cols-rebaseline-2026-08.jsonl`), frontier (`gpu-pareto-16M-2026-08.jsonl`), and airline (`airline-2026-08.jsonl`). All four rendered pages got the split, plus the README standings block and the ledger landing's division summary (both source `_division_summaries()`).

**Form chosen, by table shape:**

- **Rows and width standings** (`perf-scale.md`, `perf-shape.md`,
README): these already carry 8 variant columns in the fit table. Adding three columns per variant would have made the table wider than the page, so I added a **companion table** directly below the fit table, same row/column shape, with a `"1.1s / 6.9s"` cell (ingest / train). Column count does not grow; only row count does.
- **GPU frontier** (`perf-frontier.md`): this table was already flat
(variant, iters, fit_s, r2), so I added `ingest_s` and `train_s` as **two more columns** directly. No width pressure there, and it keeps every number for one row in one line.
- **Airline** (`perf-airline.md`): the existing convention there is
already a two-number cell (`fit_s / auc_test`), so I matched it with a **second table** of `ingest_s / train_s` cells, at the campaign-knob protocol only (depth 8) rather than duplicating for the Pafka protocol too, to avoid a fourth table on a page that already carries two fit tables, a bar chart, and an RSS/headroom table on the neighboring pages.

All of these stayed inside the site's existing `overflow-x` table wrapper; no table gained columns beyond what the frontier table added (2), so nothing that was readable got less readable.

**What did not get the split:** the four `leafwise-*` evidence files (`leafwise-ladder`, `-stage3`, `-recheck`, `-correction`) also carry `ingest_s`/`train_s` for bonsai, but those numbers predate this issue and are exactly the ones decision 100's correction section calls out as wrong: the harness built the `Dataset` before it knew which grower would consume it, so the device arms silently binned on the host and posted an inflated ~15s ingest number describing a pipeline no CUDA grower actually runs. That is the failure mode issue #301's "Watch for" section warns about by name. Rendering a naive ingest/train column from those files would resurrect the debunked number inside the correction narrative that already exists to retire it. Those sections' own prose already explains the harness bug at length; I left them untouched rather than re-opening that story.

The `xgb33-recheck`, `wide-cpu-hist`, `cuda-wide-recheck`, single-card ceiling, campaign-smoke, and probe tables don't carry `ingest_s` at all (checked via `grep -l '"ingest_s"' benchmarks/results/*.json*`), so there was nothing to add there.

## Nulls and the CatBoost caveat

`split_str()` returns the house `-` marker when either half is `None`, never `0.0s` or a blank cell, so a null split can't be misread as a measured zero. Every table that gained the split also gained one sentence explaining why bonsai's column reads `-` (fused `train()` has no seam yet, refresh is a separate change tracked by #301) and, on every table where CatBoost's ingest appears, the caveat that `Pool()` only wraps the arrays and quantization happens inside `fit` (matches the comment already in `runners.py:run_catboost`, issue #253), so its ingest reads low and the cost is really in train. A column that is `-` all the way down (bonsai's, today) reads as "not yet measured, see the sentence above" rather than as a data gap or a bug.

Division-summary prose (`_division_summaries()`, feeding both the ledger landing and the README) now names what the *reference* libraries' split shows at 16M rows (XGBoost-GPU's ingest is most of its total, CatBoost's train is most of its). It does not claim anything about bonsai's own ingest/train balance or about cross-hardware scaling, since bonsai's split is still null in every committed file and the issue's own two-host illustration is a single run per host, not a standing. I deliberately did not transcribe the issue's or its comment's literal tables into generated docs for that reason: the ledger renders only from committed jsonl, and neither of those tables is a committed data file.

## Hand-checked arithmetic

**`rebaseline-2026-08.jsonl`, 16M rows x 100 cols, `xgb_cuda`** (used in the rows split table, README, and `perf-scale.md`): the three raw reps are `(ingest=28.633, train=7.036, fit=35.669)`, `(30.118, 7.035, 37.153)`, `(30.327, 7.104, 37.431)`. The renderer picks the min-`fit_s` rep, `35.669`, whose `ingest_s + train_s = 28.633 + 7.036 = 35.669 = fit_s` exactly. Rendered cell: `28.6s / 7.0s` (rounds `28.633` -> `28.6`, `7.036` -> `7.0`), matching what's in the diff.

**`cols-rebaseline-2026-08.jsonl`, 1M rows x 4096 cols, `catboost_gpu`** (used in the width split table, `perf-shape.md`): the two raw reps are `(ingest=4.64, train=44.016, fit=48.655)` and `(4.508, 43.946, 48.454)`. Min `fit_s` is `48.454`, from the second rep: `4.508 + 43.946 = 48.454 = fit_s`. Rendered cell: `4.5s / 43.9s`, matching the diff.

## Verification

- `python3 scripts/render_results.py` then a second
`python3 scripts/render_results.py --check`: byte-stable.
- `make docs-check`: green (results ledger, params, make-map, timeline
all in sync; docs-lint 0 hard findings; standings decision gate ok).
- `make lint-python`: clean.
- No pod rental used or needed; every number above traces to a
committed jsonl file already in the repo.

## Deviations from the brief

None that I'm aware of. Files owned by PR #299 and by the concurrent runner/A-B agent (`python/bonsai/bench/runners.py`, `python/tests/bench/test_runners.py`, `scripts/standings_ab.py`, `docs/method/benchmark-protocol.md`, `src/python/module.cpp`, `include/bonsai/dataset.hpp`, `src/bin_mappers.cpp`, `src/dataset.cpp`) were not touched.

items.title: fix(docs): correct the #82 gate finding — marginal gate, not an N=465 dip
items.body:
Corrects a wrong claim published in #325. Refs #327.

## What was wrong

`docs/benchmarks/i7-12700k.md` stated the N=465 GEMM result was "**reproducible, not measurement noise**" and attributed it to the blocked GEMM's tiling interacting badly with that specific size.

The evidence backing that was invalid in two ways:

1. The three "isolated repeat runs" were taken **on a loaded machine**. native-fast measured 38–40 GFLOP/s there; the same size on an idle machine measures 56.9.
2. Their ratios were compared against **sweep-protocol** ratios rather than like-for-like isolated runs at neighbouring sizes. The control that would have caught this — same protocol, neighbouring sizes, idle machine — was never run. Run since, it gives 82.1% at N=385 and 86.6% at N=545 against 79.5% at N=465, i.e. ordinary variation.

## What the data actually shows

Repeating the identical protocol (same binaries, same sweep, same pinning) on an idle machine fails the gate at a **different set of sizes**:

| N | committed run | verification re-run |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 305 | 80.6% | **78.7%** LOW |
| 385 | 80.2% | **79.0%** LOW |
| 465 | **76.3%** LOW | 82.5% |
| 545 | 80.2% | 86.0% |
| 1025 | 82.1% | **79.2%** LOW |

No size falls below threshold in both runs; per-size spread reaches 6 points. A fine sweep `433:505:8` is flat across the flagged region (58.7 GFLOP/s at N=465, neighbours 58.6–59.5).

**The gate failure is real and reproduces. Only the attribution was wrong.** native-fast averages ~82% of OpenBLAS for N ≥ 256 — inside the epic's 10–20% target — but an 80% threshold applied per-size to a single run has no margin against this variance.

## Changes

- Gate section rewritten around the two-run comparison, with the conclusion stated as a marginal gate rather than a size-specific defect.
- An explicit note recording that the earlier claim was wrong and why, so the correction is visible rather than silently rewritten.
- Caveats strengthened: a **"treat differences under ~5 points as noise"** rule, and the loaded-machine effect (~30% on absolute numbers) as its own bullet.
- Headline bullet reworded from "one reproducible dip" to the marginal-gate framing.
- `benchmarks/README.md` echoed the same claim; fixed there too.

## Verification

`npm run build` — 43 pages, unchanged. No remaining occurrences of the superseded claim.

## Follow-up

#327 tracks the substantive work: reducing measurement variance (`performance` governor, more iterations, report spread) and deciding what the gate should assert, since a per-size single-run threshold at this noise level is a coin flip.

items.title: Subset-2 chunk map for the v3 dispatcher, and an archival path for patcher runs
items.body:
Two changes on this branch. The second is the one that matters operationally.

---

# 1. An archival path for patcher runs (`dc8f780`)

The scanner has `archive-run` and `results/eval-history/scanner.jsonl`. The patcher had neither, and needs them more: `outputs.run_dir` points **outside** the repository on purpose — a per-task record pairs a bug id with a file and a line — so the run store sits on ephemeral disk with nothing durable pointing at it.

**Subset 2 was run, scored, and lost that way.** Its records, transcripts, cost and disposition histogram are gone; only the sighted per-case table survived, in the answer-key repo.

| File | |
|---|---|
| `tools/patcher/src/archive_run.py` | new — the archiver and the publishability guard |
| `tools/patcher/tests/test_archive_run.py` | new — 24 tests |
| `results/eval-history/patcher.jsonl` | new — one row, subset 2, backfilled |
| `.claude/skills/archive-patch-run/SKILL.md` | new — the runbook |
| `CLAUDE.md`, `results/README.md` | the rule, where it gets found |

### The split is enforced, not described

```
aggregate  ->  results/eval-history/patcher.jsonl   committed, publishable
located    ->  <private store>/<stamp>/             outside the repository
```

The history row is built from an **allowlist** of aggregate fields — `tasks[]` is never read, not filtered and not summarised — and the finished row is then re-checked for bug ids, challenge keys, `file:line` references, source paths, and keys that carry located material by construction. Two independent mechanisms, because a leaked row looks exactly like a clean one and gets found by a reader months later, which is how two of the four recorded breaches happened.

The guard immediately caught a false positive in my own row builder: the field holding a task *count* was named `tasks`, the same name as the located array. Renamed to `tasks_total` rather than exempted — a count sharing the array's name invites the array to be dropped in later by someone who sees the key is already there.

### The backfilled row

Cost, wall clock, harness commit, disposition histogram and blind audit are `null`, because they are gone and guessing them would put invented numbers in the only patcher record that exists. The row says so, and it says the thing most likely to be misread later: **2/10 and 10/23 effective fixes are the same patcher output scored against two different oracle sets.** The rate moved because ground truth grew 13 driver-backed oracles, not because a patch changed. The qualification travels in the row — along with the two open defects, no committed lockfile and no frozen pre-patch baseline.

Append-only, like `docs/benchmarking-results.md` and for the same reason: a correction is a new row carrying `rescore_of`, never an edit.

---

# 2. Subset-2 chunk map for the v3 dispatcher (`0e008d8`)

`tools/patcher/plan/subsets/subset-02.chunk-map.json` — 24 bugs, 8 files, 4 chunks, 3 phases, peak concurrency 2.

`plan/chunk-map.json` is generated from subset 2's bug report and pinned byte-for-byte to a fresh generation. What it lacked is the subset form the v3 dispatcher reads. The new file applies only the two documented subset steps — drop the empty bracket, renumber phases densely, drop the `depends_on` edges naming it — and changes nothing else. Derived mechanically rather than typed; `test_subset02_map.py` (25 tests) asserts each surviving chunk equals its counterpart in the generated map, and loads the file through `src/v3/chunk_map.py`, which is the code that actually reads it before a run spends anything.

| Phase | Bracket | Chunks | Agents | Tasks |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | A core | `A01` — import cycle | 1 | 7 |
| 1 | C handlers | `C01`, `C02` | 2 | 5 + 4 |
| 2 | D wiring | `D01` | 1 | 8 |

**A discrepancy this surfaced.** `subsets/README` rule 1 says chunk ids come from the full map, but no full-map artefact exists. Subset 4's `C09`/`C11` come from a full map described in prose and never generated, so `routes/metrics.ts` is `C09` there and `C02` here. Both READMEs now record it: bracket and phase granularity compares soundly across the two subsets, chunk granularity does not.

---

## Verification

`478 passed, 1 failed`. The failure is `test_subset04_map.py::test_run_config_matches_the_map`, which predates this branch and is untouched by it — it asserts the subset-4 config's `base_tree` equals the map's `tree`, and the config points at the prepared work base.

The archiver was also run end to end against a synthetic run store; the located array was absent from the emitted row. `grep -rE "\bBUG-[0-9]+\b|[a-z][A-Za-z0-9]*Challenge\b" results/ prompts/` is clean.

## Not in this change

A subset-2 run still needs a **v3 entry point** (deliberately absent — wiring it would edit a v1/v2 file), a v3 run config, a rebuilt environment, a committed lockfile, and a frozen pre-patch baseline.

items.title: feat(bench): add succinct library comparison benchmarks and ADR-0011
items.body:
## Description

This PR addresses issue #47 by adding comprehensive benchmarking and documentation for succinctly's rank/select implementation against other maintained Rust succinct-structure crates (vers-vecs, sucds, and sux). The work includes both empirical measurements and an Architecture Decision Record (ADR-0011) that records the build-vs-buy reasoning behind implementing custom succinct structures in-crate rather than depending on existing libraries.

Prior to this PR, the repository could not answer whether existing crates were evaluated or benchmarked. The documentation incorrectly claimed ~3% space overhead for the rank directory (the Poppy paper's figure, not this implementation's). This PR corrects the record with measured data and honest assessment of trade-offs.

## Type of Change
- [x] New feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) — `succinct_libs` benchmark suite
- [x] Documentation update — ADR-0011, benchmark page, corrected space overhead claims
- [x] Test coverage improvement — comparison verification in benchmark

## Related Issue
Fixes #47 — "Evaluate existing succinct crates and benchmark against them"

## Changes Made

**Benchmark Implementation:**
- Added `bench-compare/benches/succinct_libs.rs` with comprehensive rank/select comparison across four libraries
- Implemented `TrackingAllocator` for precise resident-size measurement
- Created `verify_agreement` test ensuring all four libraries agree on rank1/select1 answers before timing
- Benchmarks test construction, rank1 (10,000 random queries), select1, and resident memory across 1M-10M bits at 10/50/90% density
- Added `succinct_libs` benchmark to registry in `src/bin/succinctly/bench_runner/registry.rs`
- Updated `bench-compare/Cargo.toml` with dependencies: `vers-vecs`, `sucds`, `sux`, `rand`, `rand_chacha` (all pinned for reproducibility)
- Updated `bench-compare/Cargo.toml` to enable `simd` feature for succinctly and vers-vecs

**Documentation:**
- Created `docs/adrs/adr-0011.md` — Architecture Decision Record documenting why succinct structures are built in-crate
  - Records three requirements: `no_std` support (no existing crate satisfies), balanced-parentheses tree navigation (none provide), hinted select (none expose)
  - Honestly reports that BitVec wins no measured category on ARM64: sux is 1.5-1.7x faster at rank/select, vers-vecs is 5-8x more compact and faster to build
  - Documents why BitVec is kept despite losing: only `no_std` requirement currently holds; BalancedParens and JsonIndex bypass BitVec entirely
  - Lists alternatives evaluated and rejected (vers-vecs, sux, sucds, succinct, fid, bio) with rationale
- Created `docs/benchmarks/rust-succinct-libs.md` — benchmark results and methodology
  - Platforms: ARM64 only (Apple M5 Max); flags x86_64 run as outstanding
  - Resident size table: vers-vecs 5-8x more compact; succinctly 27.5-47.5% overhead rising with density
  - Construction: vers-vecs 1.0-1.31x faster
  - rank1: succinctly 1.8-2.3x faster than vers-vecs, but sux 1.5-1.7x faster than succinctly
  - select1: sux 3-4x faster; marked as noisy (~40% variance in individual cells)
  - Documents fairness caveat: sucds/sux lack bulk-word constructor, must fill per-bit
- Updated `docs/adrs/README.md` to add ADR-0011 entry
- Updated `docs/architecture/README.md` — noted Prior Art now includes Rust crates evaluated
- Corrected `docs/architecture/bitvec.md` — rank directory overhead documented as ~25% (128 bits per 512 bits), not ~3%; full BitVec 27.5-47.5% resident
- Comprehensively updated `docs/architecture/prior-art.md`
  - Clarified Poppy paper claims 3% but succinctly's directory costs ~25% by design
  - Added table of Rust succinct libraries with versions, `no_std` status, and assessments
  - Documented sucds `no_std` attribute is vestigial in 0.8.3 — builds fail with ~141 errors
  - Cross-referenced ADR-0011 and benchmark page
- Updated `docs/benchmarks/README.md` — added rust-succinct-libs row to benchmark table
- Updated `docs/benchmarks/inventory.md` — added rust-succinct-libs.md (4 sections)
- Updated `docs/log.md` with 2026-07-15 entry documenting sources ingested and corrections made
- Updated `docs/optimizations/cache-memory.md` — rank directory overhead corrected from 3% to ~25%
- Updated `docs/optimizations/hierarchical-structures.md` — rank/select overhead corrected to reflect actual measurements
- Updated `CLAUDE.md` — BitVec performance summary corrected from ~3-4% to ~28-48% overhead
- Updated `README.md` — corrected feature claims from "~3% space overhead" to "tuned for query speed over compactness (~28-48% overhead)"
- Updated README core structures documentation with link to benchmark results

## Testing

**Automated Testing:**
- [x] All existing tests pass
- [x] New benchmark suite added with verification step (`verify_agreement` ensures all four libraries agree on rank1/select1 answers)
- [x] Benchmark registered and accessible via `bench run succinct_libs` command

**Manual Testing:**
- [x] Benchmarks tested on ARM64 (Apple M5 Max)
- [x] `cargo test` passes with all benchmarks
- [x] `cargo clippy` clean
- [x] `cargo fmt` applied

### Test Commands
```bash
# Run the new benchmark suite
cd bench-compare
cargo bench --bench succinct_libs

# Or via the bench runner
succinctly bench run succinct_libs

# Verify all tests pass
cargo test --all

# Check code quality
cargo clippy --all-targets --all-features -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --check
```

## Performance Impact
- [x] No performance impact to main crate (benchmarks are in `bench-compare` standalone crate)
- Benchmark findings documented: succinctly's BitVec trades space for query speed; loses on space (vers-vecs 5-8x better), loses on select (sux 3-4x faster), competitive on rank, faster to build than sux/sucds

## Checklist
- [x] My code follows the project's style guidelines
- [x] I have performed a self-review of my own code
- [x] I have added comprehensive documentation explaining the decision
- [x] Benchmark code includes verification logic (`verify_agreement`)
- [x] New and existing tests pass locally
- [x] Documentation is complete and accurate (corrected prior misstated overhead figures)
- [x] No new warnings generated

## Additional Notes

**Honest Assessment**: This PR deliberately reports findings as they came out rather than as a defense of the existing code. The measurements show BitVec loses on space and select performance but wins on rank speed (among the measured libraries). The decision to keep it in-crate is justified by three requirements: `no_std` (which no external crate satisfies), balanced-parentheses tree navigation, and hinted select — only the first currently applies to BitVec itself. The code acknowledges that BalancedParens and JsonIndex bypass BitVec entirely, making its use a candidate for replacement (tracked in issue #228).

**Platform Limitations**: Results are ARM64-only (Apple M5 Max). Succinctly's x86_64 popcount is AVX-512 VPOPCNTDQ-gated and untested here. Vers-vecs' SIMD select is also AVX-512-gated, so an x86_64 run could change the placings and is flagged as outstanding. The resident-size measurements are deterministic and platform-independent.

**Space Overhead Corrections**: Four documents claimed ~3% overhead for the rank directory. That is the Poppy paper's figure, not succinctly's implementation. All instances have been corrected to the measured value: ~25% for the rank directory alone, 27.5-47.5% for the full BitVec with select index (rising with density). This was an arithmetic error in bitvec.md that propagated through the docs.

**Future Work**: ADR-0011 recommends revisiting this decision if the `no_std` requirement is dropped or if sucds fixes its `no_std` build. The benchmark provides a stable baseline for that future evaluation.

items.title: feat: TabArena insurance benchmark — parsimony frontier, Spanish motor extension, digest (issue #27, #27a)
items.body:
## Purpose 1 — Issue #27 benchmark deliverables (D1–D5)

Frontier benchmark comparing TabPFN (hosted API) vs GLM family vs GBDTs (RF/CatBoost/LGBM/XGBoost) on **12 insurance datasets (6 classification + 6 regression)**:

- **Runner**: `scripts/eval/insurance_benchmark_v1/run_frontier_benchmark.py` (self-contained; sklearn/lightgbm/catboost/xgboost + hosted TabPFN client; `--regression` mode)
- **Protocol**: 5-fold CV (seed 42), defaults-only models, log loss / RMSE / Poisson deviance, dominance rule = strictly fewer params AND >1 SE better (beyond-SE rule, D3)
- **Param counting**: GLMs = cols + intercept; GBDTs = n_estimators × mean leaves (fold-0); TabPFN = constant 10M (recorded non-decision, membership-invariant)
- **Outputs**: `frontier_results_<dataset>.csv` + `frontier_plot_<dataset>.png` per dataset; `home_turf_sweep_results.csv` (size sweep); `money_chart_tabpfn_relative.png` (synthesis chart)
- **Docs**: spec (`docs/analyses/insurance_frontier_benchmark_spec.md`), §14.x benchmark chapters, results digest table, non-technical one-pager (`docs/reports/TABPFN_BENCHMARK_SUMMARY.md`), benchmark portfolio + naming canon

### Headline findings

- Size sweep: TabPFN wins **8/9 cells at ≤5K rows** → small-data specialist
- Frontier: on-frontier **7/12**; off-frontier at scale **5×** (ausprivauto0405, bemtl97_amount, freMTPL2freq, spanish_motor_freq, spanish_motor_severity — all ≥53.5K rows); 21-param GLMs within noise of 10M-param TabPFN
- Lapse: TabPFN wins Spanish motor lapse at **5-fold** (AUC 0.7553 vs LGBM 0.7500, 5/5 folds) + premium regression (RMSE 19.07)
- Verdict: adopt TabPFN where data is scarce; **not** a general insurance engine

### Reproducibility

- TabPFN pinned to hosted **v3** (`model_path="v3_default"`, client 0.3.3); §12.1 documents the model-version correction (v3 API accepts 1M rows — at-scale pattern is mechanism-independent)
- `TABPFN_API_KEY` env/.env setup documented; no secrets in repo
- Pre-merge checklist: all items resolved (data/scripts READMEs, run logs force-added, rescore docstring note)

## Purpose 2 — Repo cleanup / onboarding (merged from prior cleanup PRs)

README rewrite, LICENSE, CONTRIBUTING, CHANGELOG, `.gitignore` (covers `.venv*`; drops accidental `.venv312/` commit), `.opencode/` agents + skills, notebook widget stripping, `.sty` filename renames, `outputs/archive/` + stale model artifact cleanup.

## Purpose 3 — Earlier TabArena v1 harness (same branch, pre-#27)

`scripts/run_tabarena_insurance_benchmark.py` (legacy TabArena wrapper), lapse benchmark (now 5-fold, eudirectlapse + spanish_motor_lapse), smoke test, imbalance study + their CSVs/PDFs. `results_per_split.csv` is context-only (3-fold protocol differs from the frontier runner).

## Data

7 new raw datasets (ausautoBI8999, bemtl16, bemtl97, norauto, uslapseagent + spanish_motor_freq/lapse/severity) + Spanish motor portfolio source dir + `data/raw/README` context. Note: `beMTPL16.csv` (raw CASdatasets variant, added on main) now coexists with `bemtl16.csv` (cleaned benchmark version) — different schemas, both kept. Leak exclusions documented (bemtl97 label leak §6; Spanish history-variable leak AUC 0.918; `Date_lapse` 0.85).

## Reconcile with main

Merged `origin/main` (5 additive commits: roadmap xlsx, reference PDFs, Spanish motor portfolio, beMTPL16/fretelematic datasets, Colab widget strip). Zero conflicts. Branch is 40 commits ahead, fully additive.

## Included fixes

- Removed hardcoded `/Users/Scott/...` API-key fallback from 4 scripts; README documents `TABPFN_API_KEY` setup (commit ae925b0)
- No secrets in diff (scanned); `.env` gitignored
- Known workaround: push requires `http.version=HTTP/1.1` + `http.postBuffer=524288000` (git 2.39.3 HTTP/2 upload bug) — set in this repo's config
- Note: `main` carries 2 content-neutral junk commits from a push diagnostic (`f0bf230`, `5264ec1`) — tree identical to before; cleanup pending force-push decision

## Future work (out of scope here)

Fine-tuned TabPFN in the frontier, other foundation models, context-window ensembling, re-runs on future TabPFN versions.

items.title: docs: reconcile with the five merges after #240 [OPERATOR-PR]
items.body:
`PLAN.md` was reconciled with reality in #240 (`a1bf541a`). **Five merges landed after it** and none were reflected: `79d3576d` (A.5, #239), `a9bbf40a` (docs headline set, #241), `6662d062` (A.1b, #238), `23d8a871` (A.1c + A.6, #242), `b5673f17` (B.1 Phase 1a, #243).

Verified staleness before editing: `solo-noreview` appeared **zero** times in `PLAN.md`, `STATUS.md` and `README.md`, despite being a newly measured arm with a published number. A.5 was still described as a rewrite "advisory until measured". A.6 was still forward-looking. A.1's blockers were still described as open.

**Documentation only.** No code, no tests, nothing under `bench/swebench/results-archive/`, and `bench/swebench/results.md` untouched. `uv run python bench/swebench_adapter.py report --from-archive bench/swebench/results-archive/2026-08-04T23-19-24.998844Z --check` prints **`CHECK OK`**. `uv run ruff check .` passes.

## `PLAN.md`

**Ticked**

- **A.1** — both halves. Bench half **DONE** (#238); the four blockers **CLOSED** (#242); gate-ordering test pinned (#239). `- [ ]` → `- [x]` on the bench bullet.
- **A.5** — **DONE, as a DELETION.** Section header and preamble rewritten, four diagnosis bullets ticked.
- **A.6** — **DONE**, folded into A.1c and built once as `factory/chain/red_green.py`.
- **B.1** — **Phase 1a DONE, and it has a number.**

**Corrected**

- **A.5 did not ship as this plan specified it.** The ablation branch was *deleted* from the required `tests-meaningful` gate (~200 lines), not rewritten inside it. The repaired measurement lives off the merge path (`factory/chain/mutation.py` + `factory mutation-score`), imported by no gate with a test enforcing that. Recorded the generalising reason: *advisory-by-constant is one edit from blocking every merge; advisory-by-not-being-imported is not.* New primitive `check_can_fail` documented, including that green / unattributable red / timeout / un-materializable tree are all `False` **with the reason**. `gates.mutation_testing` is inert.
- **Why the acceptance-oracle flag is still off changed.** It is no longer "the blockers are open" — it is the surviving **in-process hole** (three lines of production code reassigning pytest's test-runner function), pinned as an `xfail(strict=True)`. §0's sequencing sentence and A.1's warning block both rewritten accordingly.
- **§0's bench queue** no longer says it is blocked behind an in-flight bench PR; #238 and #243 have landed.
- **Rejected #5** ("turn on the ablation gate") marked moot — there is no longer a flag to flip.
- **`README.md`'s `report --check` command pointed at the wrong archive** — see below; logged as correction 36.

**Added**

- **§1a — a sixth arm, `solo-noreview`**, as a clearly-labelled table *adjacent* to §1's five-arm table. **The five-arm headline numbers were not touched**, and the new section says why it is published separately. Six interpretation limits stated at the same prominence as the number.
- **A.1** — the A.1b independence exposure found on live data (the dev's filesystem search named the acceptance store; the detector refused the row), plus the three generalising defects from the two adversarial passes (errors-only base red laundering a tautology; `pyproject.toml`'s dual role and the *measured-wrong* empty-config mechanism; the non-authoritative-error standing rule).
- **B.1 — the settled, operator-approved production design**, so the next agent does not redesign it: `chain_mode: solo` read in exactly one place, blast radius zero for in-flight stories, iteration-neutral horizon with the one timeout that must move (1800 s → 5400 s) and its loop-cap ceiling test, the hard coupling to `gates.acceptance_oracle: true`, and **the pre-committed restraint** — do not flip the default on loop 1 before C.3 reports.
- **Corrections 30–36**, in the section's existing style.

## `STATUS.md`

- Title extended; a "read the reviewer ablation next" paragraph after the provenance note.
- **New section: "The reviewer ablation — measured 2026-08-05, `solo-noreview`"** — the table, the paired statistic, and the interpretation limits as their own subsection.
- **New section: "Fixed 2026-08-05 (Phase A — the verification layers)"** — an eight-row was-broken/now/PR table covering A.5's gate deletion, the off-merge-path measurement, `check_can_fail`, A.1b's authoring + the live independence exposure, A.1c/A.6's red→green and the five lower-ranked defects, and the gate-ordering test. Plus the three generalising adversarial findings.
- **New subsection: "The acceptance oracle's real status: executable, hardened, and still OFF"** — with the flip prerequisites.

items.title: Correct the EU AI Act Art.15 date (AI Omnibus) + re-cut the determinism evidence
items.body:
Two independent corrections, split into two reviewable commits.

## 1. `fix(compliance)` — EU AI Act Article 15 application date (AI Omnibus)

The repo asserted in seven live places that Article 15 becomes binding on
`2026-08-02` — the original Regulation (EU) 2024/1689 Article 113 staging. The
**AI Omnibus Regulation** (OJ L_202601744, in force July 2026) moved those dates.
Per the European Commission's AI Act page (last updated 2026-07-27):

> the rules for high-risk AI systems embedded into regulated products (Annex I)
> have an extended transition period until 2 August 2028 and the rules for
> high-risk use cases in certain sensitive areas (Annex III) have been extended to
> 2 December 2027 as a result of the political agreement on the proposal to
> simplify the AI Act – 'AI Omnibus'

So the corrected dates are **Annex III high-risk → 2027-12-02** and **Annex I
product-embedded → 2028-08-02**. Corrected the `AAK-EU-AI-ACT-ART15-LOCALE-001`
finding evidence, its rule description and module docstring, the `compliance.py`
Article-15 evidence subsection, and the README Legal Compliance row; regenerated
`rules.json` (rule count unchanged, 273). Tests assert the new date and guard that
the superseded date cannot silently return. Severity stays INFO / no OWASP-Agentic
tag, so the control status is unchanged. The previously shipped date was
**superseded by a regulation change, not invented** — the historical 0.3.x
CHANGELOG entry recording it is left intact.

Sources:
- Commission AI Act page: https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/policies/regulatory-framework-ai
- AI Omnibus Regulation (OJ L_202601744): https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=OJ:L_202601744

## 2. `chore(bench)` — re-cut the determinism evidence + add a freshness fence

`benchmarks/determinism/RESULTS.md` still stamped "AAK v0.3.46 (231 rules)" — 18
releases and 42 rules behind HEAD — with a SHA-256 that no longer reproduced on
the shipped version. Re-cut at v0.3.65 (273 rules); the digest changed
(`199278f2…` → `189055d0…`) and findings/run went 9 → 10 **because the rule set
grew, not because determinism regressed** (still one shared digest, 0% variance).
Added `test_published_results_md_matches_live_run` — the freshness fence that did
not exist — which ties the published header + digest to a live run and fails with
the exact regenerate command, so the artifact cannot re-stale without failing CI.

Bumps 0.3.64 → 0.3.65.

## Gates
`ruff check .` clean · `mypy agent_audit_kit` clean · full `pytest` green except
the README-pin-vs-newest-tag guard, which is red until `v0.3.65` is tagged (by
design — it reminds you to cut the tag) and goes green once the tag lands.

items.title: Move engineering docs to spec/, resync with the implementation, and group the tree
items.body:
## Summary

- move internal engineering documentation from `docs/engineering/` to a root-level `spec/` directory, and define that tree in `CLAUDE.md` as the source of truth that must stay synchronized with the implementation
- resync the tree with the code: ~100 claims that no longer matched shipped behavior
- add coverage for three surfaces that had no specification at all
- group the 15 top-level documents into `api/`, `design/`, `matplotlib/`, `benchmarks/` and `process/`, and rewrite `spec/README.md` as a real index
- update every path consumer: build inputs, CI output paths, packaging rules, tests, generator scripts, and code comments

## Why

The engineering documents are internal specifications rather than public docs-site content. Moving them to a top-level `spec/` directory makes that role explicit.

But promoting a tree to "source of truth" only helps if it is true. Auditing all 24 documents against the implementation found the tree had drifted at PR #96 — five behavior PRs (#103, #105, #106, #108, #115) landed with no spec update. Three architecture documents described systems that no longer exist. Shipping the rename without that resync would have made the tree authoritative and wrong at the same time, so the first contributor to follow it would write wrong code.

## Accuracy

Representative corrections, each verified against code:

- `spec/design/rust-engine.md` — ABI v31 → v36; "zero-crate cdylib" → `png` is a real dependency; pyramid ABI names (`xy_pyramid_tile`/`_poll` do not exist; shipped names are `_count`/`compose`/`append`); the panic shield was listed as pending but landed 29 ABI bumps ago as `ffi_guard`
- `spec/design-dossier.md` §3/§8 — described a Rust→WASM/Web-Worker/SharedArrayBuffer core; the shipped core is a C-ABI cdylib loaded by ctypes, as the same document's §32 already said. Reconciled, with the dropped WASM path recorded so the history is not lost
- `spec/design/renderer-architecture.md` — R2 claimed "No VAOs" via a `_bindScalarAttr` that does not exist; `gl.createVertexArray()` ships
- `spec/matplotlib/compat.md` — claimed the shim adds "+9% at 10k"; the guardrail it cites as proof says +60%
- `spec/benchmarks/results.md` — Plotly `Scattergl` at 10M appeared as both 54,064 ms and 33,907 ms from the same run; the derived headline multiplier was recomputed from the correct figure
- tier selection, `ty check` gate status, browser gate count, and the CI-enforced bundle budget corrected to match what CI actually does

## Coverage

New documents for surfaces with zero prior coverage:

- `spec/api/export.md` — the static export surface shipped in #115 (`to_image`/`write_image`/`write_images`, five formats, `Engine.auto` routing). Records screen/export theme parity as an open gap rather than implying it is solved
- `spec/api/interaction.md` — `interaction_config()`, the event payloads, linking, and the gesture map (#103/#105)
- `spec/design/wire-protocol.md` — the eight client↔Python request kinds and the packed-vs-split first-paint layout

Also added: the `config.py` threshold table (`CLAUDE.md` §28 promises every tier decision is recorded in the spec), full JS and Rust module inventories, and the hexbin centers-only wire contract that three renderers must expand identically — previously bound only by code comments, and once the cause of a CI-red payload regression.

## Structure

```
spec/
  README.md              index of the whole tree
  design-dossier.md      entry point, cited by section number from code
  api/                   api-examples, chart-kind-contract, chart-roadmap,
                         styling, export, interaction
  design/                chart-grammar, lod-architecture, reflex-integration,
                         reflex-shaped-api, renderer-architecture, rust-engine,
                         wire-protocol
  matplotlib/            compat, compat-matrix, compat-changelog, shim-todo
  benchmarks/            results, metrics, methodology
  process/               contributing, production-readiness, security-audit
  assets/
```

`spec/README.md` previously listed only the two SVG assets, leaving 21 of 22 documents unreachable from any entry point; it is now a full index.

`scripts/verify_sdist.py` pinned only 5 top-level `spec/*.md`, so the sdist could have silently lost `spec/design/` or `spec/assets/` and still passed. It now asserts markdown under every subdirectory and both SVG snapshots.

## Validation

Run locally on this branch:

- 1,908 tests pass, 78 skipped (`tests/` and `tests/pyplot`)
- ruff 0.15.8 `format --check` and `check` both clean
- `sync_matplotlib_compat.py --check` exits 0 after the generator was repointed to the new location and link depth
- `verify_sdist.py` passes against a fresh sdist; the sdist contains all 27 `spec/` files, verified by diffing its member list against the working tree in both directions
- `check_claim_guardrails.py` and `verify_ci_workflow.py` exit 0
- every markdown link and anchor in `spec/` resolves (170 targets, checked with `test -e` from each containing file); zero repo-wide hits for any old spec path or for `docs/engineering`

Not verified locally: the benchmark regression gate. `check_regressions.py` needs fresh bench JSONs from a built engine plus Chrome/CDP, which do not run in this environment — CI has to confirm it. The `--emit-md` target and artifact upload path in `ci.yml` were repointed to `spec/benchmarks/metrics.md` and cross-checked against `verify_ci_workflow.py`'s assertions, and a repo-wide grep confirms no writer still targets the old path, but the gate itself is unproven until CI runs.

items.title: Frontier benchmark v1: pipeline, first 13-model run, and s5/chain claim corrections
items.body:
## What this is

FactWorld is a **composition instrument**. Recall is well tested by MQAR; state tracking by the S5 word-problem literature. This instrument tests **both, independently and in composition** — identically for frontier models over OpenRouter and for local from-scratch architectures, so it can (a) place a new frontier model and (b) attribute capabilities to architectural and training choices. Natural-language surface, constrained vocabulary; canonical statement in [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/ianbarber/factworld/blob/benchmark/frontier-v1/AGENTS.md).

**Components:** recall (`recall_copy`, a deferred-readout MQAR variant; parametric variant for local models) · state tracking (`binding` = last-write-wins; `s5` = non-abelian). **Compositions:** `composite` (state × recall — headline statistic is the **gap** = binding − composed) · `chain` (recall∘recall, depth at fixed breadth). **Axes:** solve rate, pool/breadth, depth/length, instant-vs-thinking regime, reasoning-token cost. **Thesis:** no element is free — each capability is paid for by an architectural or training choice.

## Current results (9-model roster, two regimes)

| Model | recall | binding @L16 | composed @L16 | composed @L64 | **gap** | chain d128 (thinking) | s5 @L256 (thinking) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| claude-opus-4.8 | 1.00 | 0.78 | 0.72 | 0.43 | **+0.06** | 0.08 | ⊘ >budget |
| claude-sonnet-5 | 0.97 | 0.77 | 0.62† | 0.32† | +0.15† | 0.04 | ⊘ >budget |
| gpt-5.5 | 1.00 | 0.80 | 0.46 | 0.33 | **+0.34** | 0.36 | 0.96 |
| kimi-k2.6 | 1.00 | 0.94† | 0.77† | 0.93† | +0.17† | 0.64‡ | 0.88 |
| gemini-3.5-flash | 1.00 | 0.66\* | 0.64\* | 0.28\* | +0.02\* | 0.88 | 0.52 |
| glm-5.2 | 1.00 | 0.70† | 0.35† | 0.16 | +0.35† | 0.36 | 0.88 |
| deepseek-v4-pro | 1.00 | 0.51 | 0.44 | 0.19 | +0.07 | ⊘ >budget | ⊘ >budget |
| qwen3.7-max | 1.00 | 0.51 | 0.24 | 0.08 | +0.27 | 0.96 | 0.80 |
| nemotron-3-ultra | 1.00 | 0.49 | 0.33 | 0.12 | +0.16 | ⊘ >budget | ⊘ >budget |
| *recency heuristic (floor)* | — | 0.04 | 0.04 | 0.06 | — | — | — |
| *object-filter floor* | — | 0.41 | 0.41 | 0.15 | — | — | — |

† visible working on the instant attempt · \* can't disable reasoning · ‡ provider ignored the token cap · ⊘ majority of calls hit the budget · replicate noise ≤ ±0.06 · gap interpretable only where binding clears the 0.41 floor

**Readings:** opus composes essentially for free (gap = noise); gpt-5.5 pays the largest clean deficit (+0.34) despite the best binding leg; instant and thinking rankings are near-orthogonal (Anthropic dominates in-weights composition, is weakest on deep chains; qwen/flash mirror it). With reasoning on, composed is ~ceiling at these settings, so the thinking regime reads through the state-stress rows. **Local** (RTX 5090, d256): composed floors for flat training; the local deficit sits on the value/recall leg — the *opposite* leg to frontier models.

**Read more:** [`reports/frontier-benchmark.md`](https://github.com/ianbarber/factworld/blob/benchmark/frontier-v1/reports/frontier-benchmark.md) (narrative) · [`docs/benchmark/results.md`](https://github.com/ianbarber/factworld/blob/benchmark/frontier-v1/docs/benchmark/results.md) (every number/mark/figure) · `docs/experiments/README.md` §6–13 (how each protocol choice was validated)

## What this PR changes

1. **The benchmark pipeline**: pinned 9-model OpenRouter registry, resumable runner with full provenance (per-example tokens/finish reasons, escalation records, cost guards), figure/table/HTML renderer. New model = one registry entry + one command (~$1–3).
2. **Task fixes, adversarially found**: the chain task's cycle-wrap defect (depth ≥ k measured a shortcut — gated + rebuilt at fixed breadth); the composite/binding recency defect (v1 family retired, de-skewed v2 shipped; re-measuring older published numbers = issue #11); markdown-blind scoring; escalation/budget confounds. Every headline artifact was independently recomputed after each fix.
3. **Measurement protocol**: answer contracts for the instant regime, explicit budgets + published empty rates for thinking, floors as first-class rows, plain-language marks, calibration probes for operating points (experiment log §12).
4. **The story docs**: `AGENTS.md` (canonical framing), `reports/frontier-benchmark.md`, restructured README, experiment log §6–13.
5. Roster decisions: llama-4, gpt-5.4, gemini-3.1-pro dropped; x-ai unrepresented (documented provider pathologies).

Spend across all runs/pilots/probes: ~$127. Late additions, all landed: **recall under load** (pool-64: all 9 models at 1.00 vs 0.016 chance — frontier recall is free even under load, making components-cheap/composition-costly a measured claim); **the chain regime contrast** (same items, d16: instant floors at 0.00–0.32, thinking scores 1.00 for 7/9 — multi-hop needs reasoning, measured within-item); **fprm on the v2 tasks** (leads the binding leg through B16, breaks at B24; its retired-v1 flagship magnitude did not carry — ordering survived, the magnitude was recency credit); and the canonical framing doc, [`AGENTS.md`](https://github.com/ianbarber/factworld/blob/benchmark/frontier-v1/AGENTS.md).
